title: MB5-03321
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Senegal, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on July 22, 2015, rejecting his refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Senegal, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on July 22, 2015, rejecting his refugee protection claim. He is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the RPD's determination and allow the refugee protection claim or, alternatively, to refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination or to hold a new hearing before the RAD.
The appellant did not submit new evidence within the meaning of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The Minister did not intervene on appeal.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination to the effect that the appellant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.

In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that because of his sexual orientation he fears for his life if he were to return to Senegal. He allegedly discovered that he is homosexual in 2013, at the age of 25. In an amendment to his BOC Form, the appellant alleges that he discovered that he is homosexual at the age of 17. Also, he had to shut down his business, which he had run from 2009 to XXXX 2012, because people suspected that he was homosexual. In XXXX 2013, he supposedly met a man named XXXX, with whom he began a secret relationship. He states that in XXXX 2014, some young people who thought he was strange prevented him from entering a mosque. In XXXX 2014, his mother supposedly told him it was time he got married and, at that point, he told her that he was interested in men, not women. Seeing his mother's anger, he purportedly fled to his paternal grandfather's house and, from that point on, the appellant noticed that people's attitude towards him changed.

On XXXX XXXX, 2014, at about 11 p.m., some young people allegedly walked in on him and XXXX during an intimate moment. He says that he was beaten and that he fled. He then purportedly went to a friend's house in Dakar, the capital, and that friend helped him obtain a passport and leave Senegal. He left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2014, and arrived in Canada the next day on a Canadian visa that he obtained in XXXX 2014.

In its decision rendered on July 22, 2015, the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim, finding that the appellant's testimony was not credible because it was often confused and inconsistent, for the reasons that can be summarized as follows: o With respect to his alleged sexual orientation: The RPD noted that the appellant amended his original account regarding the age he discovered that he is homosexual, i.e. 17, and the appellant was unable to explain why, in his BOC Form, he indicates that it was at the age of 25. In addition, there are omissions in his BOC Form concerning significant events that took place when the appellant was young and concerning the death threats he allegedly received between 2009 and 2012 because he is homosexual. o There is an inconsistency to the effect that people suspected he is homosexual, considering that he dated women and did not meet up with men, and the appellant's response does not explain that inconsistency. In addition, the appellant testified that he had to hide-and hide his personality in particular-once it was discovered that he is homosexual, but he was unable to do so. o With respect to his relationship with XXXX: The RPD noted that the appellant's testimony was strained and he gave three different versions as to when he admitted he was sexually attracted to XXXX. In addition, the RPD found that the appellant's testimony was contradictory with respect to how often he met with XXXX. It also concluded that it is implausible that it took 15 months for the appellant to ask XXXX if he was interested in an intimate relationship, despite the fact that he was attracted to him. o With respect to the attack on XXXX XXXX, 2014, which allegedly took place at XXXX home in XXXX, it is implausible that the aggressors fled because they were worried about problems with the neighbours, given that they live in a society where homosexuality is banned and severely punished. There are inconsistencies concerning when the appellant left for Dakar and the lack of contact with XXXX after the alleged attack. o There was an inconsistency in the appellant's testimony to the effect that he did not return to XXXX after the attack of XXXX XXXX, 2014, yet he obtained his national identity card, which was registered in XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The documentary evidence indicates that the applicant must be physically present when both applying for and picking up the card. The RPD noted its preference for the documentary evidence, which contradicts the claimant's testimony. o There is an inconsistency concerning the address in XXXX that the appellant provided in order to obtain a visa. The appellant testified that he was living at a friend's home in Dakar at that time. o The RPD had serious doubts about the appellant's testimony to the effect that he was unaware of the similarities among the refugee protection claims of the people he was travelling with, who also invoked fear of persecution by reason of their sexual orientation. o The appellant's credibility was undermined by the fact that he waited more than two months before claiming refugee protection in Canada. o The RPD concluded that it did not believe the story about the appellant's sexual orientation or the fact that he had been persecuted in his country as alleged, and it granted no probative value to the documentary evidence submitted by the appellant in support of his allegations.

In the memorandum that was submitted, the appellant's lawyer states that the RPD erred in its non-credibility findings, for the reasons that can be summarized as follows: - With respect to his sexual orientation, the appellant's explanations were credible, the RPD did not offer compelling reasons for doubting his testimony and there were no inconsistencies in his testimony. - With respect to his relationship with XXXX, the appellant described it in great detail, there are no contradictions concerning when he revealed his attraction to XXXX and there are no implausibilities with respect to the timing of his first sexual encounter. - With respect to the attack on XXXX XXXX, 2014, there is no implausibility regarding the fact that the aggressors fled, and there are no inconsistencies concerning when the appellant left XXXX. - With respect to him obtaining his national identity card, the appellant gave his personal information to a police officer. In addition, the address where he was living in hiding was not his official address for the visa and the RPD's conclusion doubting that he lived in hiding is unreasonable.
In the appellant's memorandum, the lawyer states that the appellant is not submitting new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and is requesting that a hearing be held before the RAD.

To begin, it must also be noted that, under subsection 110(3) of the IRPA, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the RPD proceedings. Also, under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, the RAD may hold a hearing when evidence presented on appeal is found to be admissible, if it raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, if it is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and if it justifies allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

In the matter at hand, the parties did not submit new evidence in accordance with subsections 110(3) and 110(4) of the IRPA; consequently, there is no cause to hold a hearing before the RAD.1 SCOPE OF THE APPEAL
It should be noted that the appellant's lawyer did not present any argument concerning the standard of intervention that the RAD should apply.
I am of the opinion that the RAD's scope must be examined in light of the IRPA and the case law on this subject.

First, the IRPA does not expressly set out the standard of intervention that the RAD should apply when reviewing RPD decisions. The introductory wording of the IRPA in subsection 110(1) is as follows: Subject to subsections (1.1) and (2), a person or the Minister may appeal, in accordance with the rules of the Board, on a question of law, of fact or of mixed law and fact, to the Refugee Appeal Division against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division to allow or reject the person's claim for refugee protection.

Furthermore, with regard to the RAD's decisions, subsection 111(1) of the IRPA provides that the RAD shall confirm the determination, set aside the determination and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, or refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.

In Huruglica, the Federal Court of Appeal determines that the RAD's role is to intervene when the RPD has made an error in law, in fact or in fact and in law.2 It also concludes that an appeal before the RAD is not a true de novo proceeding.3 In addition, it clearly indicates which approach the RAD should use: [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable.

As for the measure of deference that the RAD owes to the RPD's determinations or findings concerning the credibility of testimony, the Federal Court of Appeal also states the following in Huruglica: [70] This also recognizes that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because they require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. It further indicates that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis, In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim. [71] One can imagine many possible scenarios. For example, when the RPD finds a witness straightforward and credible, there is no issue of credibility per se. This will also be the case when the RAD is able to reach a conclusion on the claim, relying on the RPD's finding of fact regarding the relative weight of testimonies and their credibility or lack thereof. [72] Problems will occur when the credibility findings themselves are disputed on appeal, and the RAD has no way to reach a conclusion without endorsing or rejecting those findings. If the RAD can identify an error in situations where, for example, a claimant was not found credible because his story was not plausible based on common sense, the RPD may have no real advantage over the RAD. [73] Similarly, there may also be cases where a finding that a witness is not credible was based on discrepancies that could not justify such a conclusion or that simply did not exist. If the assessment of the oral evidence contains an error which the RAD can easily identify, but the weight to be given to this testimony is essential to determine whether the RPD decision should be confirmed or set aside, the RAD may conclude that it is a proper case to refer back to the RPD with specific directions in respect of the error identified in the credibility findings. [74] That said, it is not appropriate to say more about the various scenarios that may arise, for they are not before us. The RAD should be given the opportunity to develop its own jurisprudence in that respect; there is thus no need for me to pigeon-hole the RAD to the level of deference owed in each case.

Thus, it is my opinion that the RAD is a specialized tribunal and that I must conduct an independent assessment of all the evidence to determine whether the appellant is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA and, therefore, whether the RPD's decision is well founded in light of the evidence presented to the RPD, the appeal records, as well as any new evidence within the meaning of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA or any evidence gathered during a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, if applicable. In the case at hand, it should be noted that no new evidence was presented and there was no RAD hearing.

Also, in reviewing this case, I will show a measure of deference to the RPD's findings concerning the appellant's credibility that are based on his testimony. Furthermore, if there are errors on questions of law or if there are erroneous findings or findings that are not supported by the evidence on questions of fact or of mixed law and fact that are central to the claim for refugee protection, I will intervene in accordance with the provisions of subsections 111(1) and 111(2) of the IRPA.

The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in its determination. To that end, I reviewed the RPD's reasons and decision and I listened to the recording of the RPD hearing. I also read and assessed the totality of the evidence on the record, as well as the appellant's memorandum. I will address the RPD's findings while considering the appellant's arguments. RPD's findings of non-credibility a) Sexual orientation

The appellant testified that he was a homosexual in Senegal. The RPD concluded that there was his explanations were lacking concerning the change to the age at which he discovered his sexual orientation in the amended BOC Form. It also found that there were inconsistencies and omissions on that point that undermined the appellant's credibility. The appellant's lawyer argues that the appellant was credible and that there were no inconsistencies or serious reasons to doubt his credibility.

With respect to the chronology of the events alleged, based on my assessment of the recording of the RPD hearing, the appellant testified that from the age of 14 until he was 17, youth in his neighbourhood harassed him because they suspected he was homosexual. When confronted with the fact that he failed to include any such allegations in his BOC Form, the appellant explained that he wanted to say it at the hearing. The RAD considers it reasonable to believe that if these alleged difficulties were true, the appellant would have mentioned them in his BOC Form, along with the other issues he has allegedly faced. I agree with the RPD that this omission undermines the appellant's credibility.

The RPD thoroughly questioned the appellant about his discovery that he is homosexual. He testified that it was when he was approximately 17 years old, and not at the age of 25, as he indicates in his original BOC Form. When questioned as to why he did not write in his original BOC Form that he discovered he was homosexual when he was 17, the appellant stated that he could not explain it. When questioned by the RPD about how he discovered his sexual orientation at the age of 17 (in 2005), he testified that he was attracted to men. When further questioned about his discovery, the appellant reiterated that he was attracted to men and that it felt good to him. Like the RPD, the RAD is of the opinion that it is reasonable to believe that if the appellant had discovered his homosexuality at the age of 17, as he alleges, he would have mentioned it in his original BOC Form and he would have provided explanations as to why he did not do so. In addition, the RAD considers that the appellant's explanations about his discovery were vague and, although he was repeatedly questioned by the RPD, he was unable to provide any additional information. Consequently, I agree with the RPD's finding to the effect that the appellant's credibility was undermined.

The appellant testified that he sold XXXX between XXXX 2009 and XXXX 2012 and that he had to shut down his business because people suspected he was homosexual. He added that he was harassed on a daily basis and received death threats. He was suspected of being homosexual because he spent time only with women, not with men. When asked to provide further explanation on that point, the appellant testified that he always sat with the female XXXX vendors because the men harassed him.

To begin, the RAD finds it reasonable to believe that if he were being harassed on a daily basis, the appellant would have mentioned that allegation in his BOC Form, given the alleged seriousness and frequency. While the BOC Form mentions that certain individuals made indirect threats if they were to catch a homosexual, there is absolutely no mention of the appellant receiving death threats. Like the RPD, the RAD finds that those omissions further undermine the appellant's credibility. As well, it seems inconsistent that he would be suspected of begin homosexual because he visited the other female vendors, that is, members of the opposite sex, and the appellant's explanations do not explain why it was frowned upon. Consequently, I completely agree with the RPD's findings that this undermines the appellant's credibility.

The appellant testified that he had to hide after it was discovered that he is homosexual. Since the appellant continued with his business and carried out his other occupations, the RPD questioned him to find out more. The appellant testified that he had to hide his personality and that he went earlier to sell his XXXX and left earlier to go home. When questioned further, the appellant testified that he could not explain it. The RAD is of the opinion that this explanation is in no way connected to the appellant's personality and that it did not answer the RPD's questions. What is more, the appellant testified via an interpreter and there was no indication that the appellant had not understood the questions being asked. Furthermore, that possibility was not raised by the appellant's lawyer. I agree with the RPD's finding that this further undermines the appellant's credibility. b) Relationship with XXXX

The RPD concluded that the appellant had provided three versions of when he first broached the topic of homosexuality with XXXX. As well, there was a contradiction concerning how often he met with XXXX and an implausibility regarding how much time passed before they had their first sexual encounter. The appellant's lawyer argues that there is no contradiction or implausibility and that the appellant provided several details.

According to my assessment of the recording of the hearing, the RPD questioned the appellant about how he broached the topic of his sexual preference with XXXX for the first time. He first testified that he met XXXX on the beach in XXXX 2013. At that time, he was allegedly attracted to XXXX and asked for his telephone number, saying that he liked him. When questioned by the RPD about how he was able to broach the topic of his sexual preference the first time he met someone he did not know, the appellant replied that he was doubtful but that he could not hold back any longer. Then, the appellant added that he first told him in a text message, then on the telephone. When confronted with these versions, the appellant testified that he had spoken a little too quickly. Like the RPD, the RAD is of the opinion that these different versions, coupled with a lack of reasonable explanations from the appellant, undermine the appellant's credibility.

With respect to the alleged meetings with XXXX, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD's reasons are true to the appellant's testimony, which seemed confused and contradictory about the frequency of the meetings. As well, having assessed the RPD's conclusion of implausibility in light of Valtchev,4 quoted by the appellant's lawyer, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD did not err in its conclusion because it took into account the fact that the appellant demonstrated his [translation] "interest" in XXXX when they first met in XXXX 2013. Having considered all of the appellant's personal circumstances, including the frequency and his attraction to him, it is implausible that the appellant did not even consider having an intimate relationship with XXXX until they had been in a relationship for 15 months. c) Attack on XXXX XXXX, 2014

The RPD concluded that the circumstances surrounding when the appellant fled were implausible and that there were inconsistencies regarding when the appellant left and the lack of contact with XXXX after the attack. The appellant's lawyer argues that there were no implausibilities or inconsistencies.

To begin, according to my assessment of the recording of the hearing, the RPD confronted the appellant, indicating that it was surprised that the appellant had not tried to contact XXXX since the attack. In response, the appellant stated that he had lost his telephone and that he had not used someone else's because he was afraid he would be identified. In the RAD's opinion, it is reasonable to believe that if the attack had involved him and XXXX and, given the feelings he alleges he had towards XXXX, he would have demonstrated an interest in hearing news about XXXX and he would have taken steps, by telephone or otherwise, to find out about him. Like the RPD, I do not find his explanations reasonable, and the appellant's credibility is further undermined.

What is more, having assessed the conclusion of implausibility with respect to the appellant's alleged escape, in light of the documentary evidence5 which indicates, among other things, that homosexuals are stigmatized, that this sexual orientation is illegal and that individuals caught in the act may be arrested, the RAD also finds it implausible that the appellant was able to flee from six aggressors because of the noise and the fear that others would intervene.

With respect to when he left, the appellant testified that he left XXXX for XXXX by bus at 11 p.m. on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. That contradicts his testimony to the effect that he went to XXXX house at approximately 11 p.m., stayed for 25-30 minutes, and an hour later went back to his grandfather's home to gather his personal items before taking the bus to XXXX. When confronted with that contradiction, the appellant testified that the times were approximate. While the RAD is of the opinion that the time he left is a peripheral detail, considering the other reasons to doubt the appellant's credibility with respect to the attack and the lack of contact with XXXX, the RAD fully agrees with the RPD's conclusions. d) Other inconsistencies

The RPD noted inconsistencies in the appellant's testimony concerning the national identity card and the address appearing on the visa application. The appellant's lawyer argues that those inconsistencies do not exist.

According to my assessment of the recording of the hearing, the appellant testified that he did not return to XXXX after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. When confronted by the RPD about the fact that his scanned national identity card6 was issued in XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2014, and with the fact that, according to the documentary evidence,7 the appellant was physically required to be there to apply for and pick up the card, the appellant stated that he had provided the necessary documents to a police officer in XXXX and he got the card. In light of the previously mentioned reasons that lead to the finding that the appellant's testimony about several central aspects of his claim lacks credibility, the RAD prefers the objective documentary evidence that indicates that the appellant's physical presence is required to apply for and pick up the national identity card. Given that the national identity card was issued in XXXX 2014, the RAD agrees with the RPD's finding that it is not credible that the appellant did not return to XXXX.

With respect to the address included on the appellant's visa application,8 which does not correspond with the location where the appellant was living before he left Senegal, the appellant's explanations seem reasonable to me, given that the address on the national identity card and his passport was that in XXXX and not XXXX. Despite the fact that the RAD does not agree with the RPD's conclusion on this point, it is not determinative because it is not central to the refugee protection claim and because the RAD agrees with the other conclusions on central elements, including not believing the appellant's sexual orientation or that he was persecuted in the alleged circumstances, and no probative value is granted to the documentary evidence submitted in support of his refugee protection claim.

Having assessed all of the oral and documentary evidence, in light of the reasons above, and pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination to the effect that the appellant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The appeal filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX is dismissed. Louis Cousineau Me Louis Cousineau April 14, 2016 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Sajad v.
